title: Leibniz on the Problem of Evil

summaries.example: Imagine a song with a quiet part, a loud part, and one tense note. The tense note may sound bad by itself, but it might help the whole song work. Leibniz used similar ideas about harmony, while also saying that suffering and wrongdoing are real problems.
summaries.summary: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz asked a difficult question: if God is wise, good, and powerful, why does the world contain suffering, imperfection, and wrongdoing? This is called the problem of evil. Leibniz connected it with two other questions: whether people are truly free and whether God is responsible for sin. In his early work, he suggested that everything followed from God in a necessary harmony. But that view seemed to leave too little room for freedom and responsibility. In his mature view, God knew many possible worlds and chose the best whole. A world can contain limited creatures, suffering, and sin while still having the greatest overall harmony. Leibniz distinguished what God positively creates from evil understood as a lack or failure in created things. He also said God permits sin without wanting sin for its own sake, while finite creatures can be responsible for their own deficient choices. His Theodicy tried not only to defend a philosophical position but also to offer hope and encourage people to work for good.
key_ideas: Leibniz thought creation showed God’s goodness, but suffering and wrongdoing seemed to challenge that belief.
He tried to explain how God could create and sustain the world without being the wrongdoer.
His early ideas made everything seem necessary, which threatened human freedom.
His later view said this is the best possible world overall, even though it contains real local evils.
Leibniz said people can be responsible for wrongdoing because they knowingly choose what seems good to them, even when their judgment is limited.
summaries.why_it_matters: Leibniz’s ideas show how one question can connect beliefs about God, freedom, responsibility, suffering, and hope. They also teach us to notice the difference between explaining why someone holds a belief and deciding whether that explanation is convincing. The problem of evil remains an important challenge because people continue to ask how goodness and suffering fit together.

important_terms.definition: The question of how a good and powerful God can allow suffering, wrongdoing, and other kinds of evil.
A defense of God’s goodness and justice when evil exists.
The idea that something is missing or limited, rather than being a separate thing made by itself.
The ability to understand choices and choose between them.

questions_to_think_about: Can a world be best overall if some parts of it are very painful?
Does allowing a bad action make someone responsible for it?
Can a difficult experience ever contribute to a larger good without becoming good by itself?

summaries.example: Suppose a composer can choose among many complete symphonies. One version has a difficult, dissonant passage, but changing that passage would require changing the relationships among many other parts. Leibniz’s mature view compares a world to such an interconnected whole: removing one local defect might reduce the value of the entire composition. Critics can still ask whether the defect was necessary or whether a better composition was possible.
summaries.summary: Leibniz’s problem of evil is not simply the modern question of how any evil can coexist with an omnipotent and benevolent God. It concerns whether creation can reveal divine goodness while also containing suffering, imperfection, and sin. Two charges must be answered: God seems to be the author of sin because every creature and action depends on God, and God seems to have chosen a world that could have been better. Leibniz’s early attempts place evil within a harmony grounded in God’s intellect. Yet if everything follows necessarily from God, human contingency and moral responsibility become difficult to preserve. His mature theodicy therefore distinguishes absolute, or per se, necessity from hypothetical necessity and argues that other worlds remain possible. God chooses this world because perfect wisdom and goodness make the best choice morally necessary, not metaphysically forced. The world is best as an interconnected whole, whose value includes metaphysical, physical, and moral goods. Creatures are limited, and these limitations make suffering and sin possible. God positively concurs with the perfection in actions, permits sinful deficiency, and does not will sin as sin. Human beings remain morally responsible when their intelligent, spontaneous, and contingent agency becomes a deficient cause. Leibniz’s final discussion adds a practical dimension: people should neither deny evil nor passively await events, but accept the past while acting for the general good.
key_ideas: Leibniz treats the problem of evil as involving both God’s direct responsibility for sin and the question of why God did not create a less evil world.
His early Confessio philosophi explains evil through a universal harmony grounded in divine intellect, but this threatens to make events necessary and weaken freedom.
His mature position restores contingency: other worlds are possible in themselves, while God freely chooses the best world through moral necessity.
The best world is evaluated holistically. Metaphysical, physical, and moral goods must be considered together, and local imperfections may contribute to a greater harmony.
God’s antecedent will is directed toward each good separately; the consequent will chooses the best achievable combination, permitting some evil as part of that whole.
Creaturely freedom requires spontaneity, intelligence, and contingency. A finite agent can become a deficient cause of sin through limited understanding or disordered motivation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Leibniz offers a major historical model of theodicy and a detailed attempt to reconcile providence with freedom. His distinctions—especially between necessity and contingency, willing and permitting, and positive reality and privation—continue to shape debates about responsibility and divine action. Studying the view also clarifies why a philosophical defense of God may need both an abstract argument about value and a response to the human experience of suffering.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical and theological defense of God’s goodness or justice in view of evil.
The charge that God, as creator and continual sustainer of all actions, becomes morally responsible for sin.
Necessity grounded in perfect practical wisdom: God is free, but goodness decisively inclines God to choose the best.
God’s separate inclinations toward goods considered one at a time, contrasted with the final choice of the best total arrangement.
God’s active contribution to the positive or perfect features of every creaturely action, distinguished from permission of its sinful deficiency.
A cause of a deficiency or lack; Leibniz uses this idea to explain how finite creatures can be responsible for sin without creating evil as a positive reality.
A limitation or absence of perfection, rather than an independently produced positive substance.
A collection of mutually compatible possible beings and events considered as one complete arrangement.

questions_to_think_about: Does choosing the best total world excuse the inclusion of serious local suffering?
Is moral necessity compatible with meaningful freedom, or does a guaranteed choice cease to be free?
Can a person be responsible for a privation or failure rather than for a positive effect?
Does distinguishing physical concurrence from moral permission successfully separate God from authorship of sin?
What would count as evidence that a world is best when its total value cannot be observed from a limited human standpoint?

summaries.example: Think about a school play. A director may choose one complete version because changing one scene would force changes in the music, actors, and ending. A sad scene might help the whole story make sense, but that does not mean sadness is pleasant or good by itself. Leibniz thought the world was like an interconnected whole, though people can disagree about whether his comparison really explains suffering.
summaries.summary: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz’s Theodicy tried to answer the problem of evil: how can a good, wise, and powerful God create a world containing suffering, imperfection, and sin? Leibniz thought this question could not be separated from questions about human freedom and responsibility. His early writings placed evil within a necessary harmony that came from God’s understanding. This helped protect God from blame, but it made human choices seem less free. Over time, Leibniz developed a different account. He argued that God knows many possible worlds and chooses the best one. “Best” means best as a complete, connected whole, not necessarily best in every neighborhood or event. Creatures are limited, and these limits make suffering and wrongdoing possible. Leibniz described evil as a privation, or lack, within something that has positive reality. He distinguished God’s will toward individual goods from the final choice of the best arrangement. God does not desire sin as sin, though God permits it within the chosen world and contributes to the good features of actions. Human beings can still be responsible because they understand options and direct themselves toward what seems good, even when limited judgment leads them badly. Leibniz also said people should respond to suffering with both hope and active effort.
key_ideas: Leibniz believed God’s goodness could be understood by studying creation, yet suffering and sin made that belief difficult.
He faced two challenges: whether God is the author of sin and whether God should have created a better world.
His earliest answer made evil part of a necessary universal harmony, but this seemed to endanger freedom.
His later answer said God chose the best possible world, judged as a whole rather than by inspecting only its worst parts.
God wills good directly, permits sin rather than choosing it for its own sake, and creatures remain responsible for their limited choices.
Leibniz’s discussion also had a practical goal: to offer hope without telling people to stop trying to improve the world.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps us examine difficult claims about goodness, choice, and responsibility. Leibniz’s view is historically important because it tries to protect several ideas at once: God’s goodness, God’s care for creation, human freedom, and the reality of suffering. Whether the explanation succeeds is open to evaluation, but its careful distinctions show why simple answers to the problem of evil are rarely enough.

important_terms.definition: A reasoned attempt to defend God’s goodness and justice even though evil exists.
The puzzle of how God can be good and powerful if the world contains suffering and wrongdoing.
A lack or limitation of goodness or perfection, rather than a separate positive thing.
The idea that God’s choice of the best is compelled by perfect wisdom and goodness, but is not forced by outside pressure.
God’s first inclinations toward each good separately and God’s final decision about the best complete arrangement.
God’s involvement in the good or perfect part of an action while permitting its sinful part.
A cause that produces a failure or lack by not providing what is needed; Leibniz uses this to describe creaturely sin.

questions_to_think_about: Can a whole be good when some parts contain serious suffering?
Is permitting an action different from wanting it?
If God knows what someone will do, can that person still be responsible?
Should a philosophical explanation of evil also try to comfort people?
What might be lost if we judge a complicated system only by one part of it?
